title: Acute spinal cord injury
subtitle: Protect, perfuse, classify, decompress

red_flags.text: Weakness, numbness or paraesthesia in the limbs after trauma, even if it is improving.
Hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries: neurogenic shock, usually from a cervical or high thoracic injury.
Diaphragmatic breathing, a weak cough or a falling vital capacity in a cervical injury: impending respiratory failure.
Priapism or loss of anal tone in an unconscious trauma patient.
Ankylosing spondylitis or diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis with any neck or back pain after a minor fall. These spines fracture like long bones and are unstable.
Any ascending neurological level, which may signal cord oedema or haematoma and threatens the airway.

do_now.text: Primary survey with spinal motion restriction. The airway comes first; manual in-line stabilisation during intubation.
Treat hypotension. Exclude haemorrhage before attributing it to neurogenic shock; both can coexist.
Log-roll with adequate staff, and remove the patient from a hard board as soon as practical to protect skin.
Urgent imaging: CT of the injured region, and MRI for neurological deficit to define cord compression.

assess.text: Full ISNCSCI examination: key muscles, light touch and pin prick in every dermatome, deep anal pressure and voluntary anal contraction.
Record the neurological level and the AIS grade. Sacral sparing decides complete versus incomplete, and changes the prognosis.
Clear the cervical spine with a validated rule in an alert, unintoxicated patient without distracting injury.
Repeat the examination. An early examination in spinal shock can underestimate what is preserved.

investigate.text: CT of the whole spine in a high-energy injury or a known spinal fracture, because non-contiguous fractures are common.
MRI to assess cord compression, cord signal, disc and ligament injury, and epidural haematoma.
CT angiography of the neck when the fracture pattern or mechanism suggests vertebral artery injury, per local protocol.
Baseline vital capacity and blood gas in cervical injury; repeat them, because respiratory function can deteriorate over days.

resuscitate.text: Augment mean arterial pressure. AANS/CNS suggests 85 to 90 mmHg for the first 7 days; follow the spinal unit target, with fluids then vasopressors.
Treat symptomatic bradycardia in high cervical injury, which can follow suctioning or turning, per local protocol.
Insert a urinary catheter early; the bladder is areflexic and over-distension causes harm.
Anticipate ventilatory failure in cervical injury, and intubate electively rather than in extremis.

definitive.text: Early surgical decompression, within 24 hours of injury where feasible, for a compressed cord.
Closed reduction of a cervical facet dislocation in an awake, examinable patient, or open reduction, per the spinal surgeon's plan.
Methylprednisolone is not routine. AANS/CNS advise against it; AO Spine offers a 24-hour infusion started within 8 hours as an option. Decide with the spinal surgeon.
Stabilise unstable injuries and begin pressure, bladder, bowel and venous thromboembolism care from day one.

escalate.text: Contact the regional spinal surgical team and spinal cord injury centre on the day of injury, before transfer is needed.
Intensive care for cervical and high thoracic injuries with any respiratory compromise or haemodynamic instability.
Any deterioration in neurological level is an emergency: repeat MRI and inform the spinal surgeon immediately.

notes: The worst missed spinal injury is in the patient with a stiff spine and a trivial fall. Image them, and image the whole spine.
Neurogenic shock is warm and slow. A cold, tachycardic trauma patient with a cord injury is still bleeding until proven otherwise.
Classify with ISNCSCI, not with impressions. 'Weak legs' cannot be compared tomorrow; an AIS grade and a level can.
